reconcile.connective: Gill treats Matthew's "cried again" as a second utterance, making Luke's and John's sayings sequential last words rather than rival, exclusive ones.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman presses the point hardest: harmonizing Matthew, Luke, and John into "seven last words" erases what each evangelist individually meant to say.

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.work: Jesus, Interrupted: Revealing the Hidden Contradictions in the Bible (And Why We Don't Know About Them)

excerpts.excerpt_text: Jesus, when he had cried again,.... "A second time", as the Persic version; for he had cried once before, and expressed the words he did, as in Mat 27:46, what he now delivered were, "Father, into thy hands I commend my Spirit", Luk 23:46, and "it is finished", Joh 19:30, which he said with a loud voice …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill directly harmonizes all three 'last words' passages by reading Matthew's second cry as encompassing both Luke's and John's sayings, resolving the divergence via sequence rather than conflict.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on Matthew 27:49
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this exact passage, reading the 'cried again' of Matthew 27:49 as a second utterance that includes both Luke's and John's sayings — the harmonization keyed directly to the verse.

link.title: CARM: What are the very last words of Jesus?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment arranging the three sayings chronologically (Matthew/Mark, then John, then Luke as the final word) to resolve the 'different last words' tension.
